claim: In the medaka genome, ndrg1 has two paralogs: ndrg1a (ENSORLG00000003558) on chromosome 11 and ndrg1b (ENSORLG00000004785) on chromosome 16, with 60% identity.
source: ndrg1 belongs to the n-myc downstream regulated gene 1 family, and in the medaka genome has two paralogs (Figure 1A), as a result of teleost-specific genome duplication (Kasahara et al., 2007): ndrg1a (ENSORLG00000003558) on chromosome 11 and ndrg1b (ENSORLG00000004785) on chromosome 16, with 60% identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A showing the phylogenetic relationships, and is cited to Kasahara et al., 2007 for the teleost-specific genome duplication.

claim: The ndrg1a transcripts were not detectable in the medaka gonads during embryo developmental stages by whole-mount RNA in situ hybridization.
source: The ndrg1a transcripts were not detectable in the medaka gonads during embryo developmental stages by whole-mount RNA in situ hybridization (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-mount RNA in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The medaka ndrg1b was specifically observed in gonads during embryo developmental stages.
source: In contrast, the medaka ndrg1b was specifically observed in gonads during embryo developmental stages (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-mount RNA in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No difference for ndrg1b transcript levels was detected between female and male individuals at stage 35.
source: The transcript level of ndrg1b was quantified by qPCR at stage 35, when female (XX) and male (XY) gonads appear morphologically indistinguishable and germ cells only show type I proliferation. No difference for ndrg1b transcript levels was detected between female and male individuals (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At stage 39 and 10 dph, the level of ndrg1b transcripts is higher in male than in female gonads.
source: At stage 39 and 10 dph, where female gonads have higher number of cysts compared to male gonads due to type II cystic division, the level of ndgr1b transcripts is higher in male than in female gonads (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: At 20 dph, the level of ndrg1b transcripts is higher in female than in male gonads.
source: The opposite sex transcriptional profile of ndrg1b was observed at 20 dph (Figure 1G), when type II proliferation begins in male individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The transcription of ndrg1b is inversely related to the cystic proliferation of EGSCs in both sexes.
source: These results showed that the transcription of ndrg1b is inversely related to the cystic proliferation of EGSCs in both sexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the qPCR data showing opposite expression patterns between sexes at different developmental stages when cystic proliferation differs.

claim: In exposed females to A83-01, no difference in total EGSCs was observed compared to control.
source: When total EGSCs were quantified, in exposed females no difference was observed, but an increase in EGSCs in exposed males was observed compared to control males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In exposed males to A83-01, an increase in EGSCs was observed compared to control males.
source: When total EGSCs were quantified, in exposed females no difference was observed, but an increase in EGSCs in exposed males was observed compared to control males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No difference in ndrg1b mRNA levels was detected between control and A83-01 treatment for female individuals.
source: Additionally, no difference in ndrg1b mRNA levels was detected between control and treatment for female individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Male individuals showed increased levels of ndrg1b following TGF-β inhibitor treatment when compared to control.
source: In contrast, male individuals showed increased levels of ndrg1b following TGF-β inhibitor treatment when compared to control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), establishing that there is no negative feedback from ndrg1b via TGF-β.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The TGF-β pathway is not involved in type II proliferation in medaka.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the TGF-β pathway is not involved in type II proliferation in medaka.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that TGF-β inhibition does not affect type II proliferation in females and the lack of negative feedback on ndrg1b expression.

claim: The mutagenesis efficiency reached 96.6% for sg1_ndrg1b and 80% for sg2_ndrg1b.
source: The mutagenesis efficiency for each sgRNA was analyzed by a heteroduplex mobility assay (HMA; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Ota et al., 2013), which reached 96.6% for sg1_ndrg1b and 80% for sg2_ndrg1b (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by HMA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, with citation to the HMA method (Ota et al., 2013).

claim: None of the embryos analyzed had indels at the analyzed off-target sites for the injected sgRNA of biallelic mutant.
source: None of the embryos analyzed had indels at the analyzed off-target sites for the injected sgRNA of biallelic mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by off-target analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The screening of F2 individuals did not reveal homozygous mutants of ndrg1b.
source: However, the screening of F2 individuals by means of HMA using genomic DNA from a fin clip (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, D) did not reveal homozygous mutants of ndrg1b (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by HMA screening data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, C, and D.

claim: The total number of EGSCs in male sgN1b was unchanged with respect to the male wt individuals.
source: The total number of EGSCs in male sgN1b was unchanged with respect to the male wt individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of EGSCs in female sgN1b was significantly reduced compared to female wt individuals, decreasing to a level similar to male wt.
source: In females, however, the number was significantly reduced in female sgN1b compared to the female wt individuals (Figure 2D), decreasing to a level similar to male wt.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only type II cystic proliferation was altered in female mutants compared with wt female individuals.
source: Moreover, when the number of type I and II germ cells in mutants was quantified, only type II cystic proliferation was altered in female mutants compared with wt female individuals (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The number of EGSCs inside each cyst in sgN1b females was lower than in wt.
source: Furthermore, the number of EGSCs inside each cyst in sgN1b females was lower than in wt (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of proliferating type II germ cells was reduced in female sgN1b when compared to female wt.
source: PCNA immunostaining (Figure 2B, C) revealed that the number of proliferating type I and type II germ cells/total number of germ cell at stage 39 did not differ among female sgN1b and male gonads, but the number of proliferating type II germ cells was reduced in female sgN1b when compared to female wt (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCNA immunostaining data shown in Figures 2B, C, and G.

claim: TUNEL-positive cells were not observed in any sgN1b or wt individuals.
source: In a TUNEL assay, positive cells were not observed in any sgN1b or wt individuals (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: Female ndrg1b mutants have fewer proliferating germ cells at stage 39.
source: Hence, female ndrg1b mutants have fewer proliferating germ cells at stage 39.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the PCNA immunostaining data showing reduced proliferating type II germ cells and the absence of apoptosis.

claim: Type II cystic proliferation is affected in ndrg1b mutants.
source: These results indicate that type II cystic proliferation is affected in ndrg1b mutants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing reduced germ cell numbers, reduced proliferation, and absence of apoptosis in mutants.

claim: Individuals injected with sg2_ndrg1b showed the same loss of cystic proliferation as sgN1b biallelic mutants.
source: In addition, we performed an extra check of the efficacy of the loss of function of ndrg1b with the sgN1b guide by analyzing the phenotype of loss of cystic proliferation in individuals injected with a second RNA guide, sg2_ndrg1b. We observed the same results as the sgN1b biallelic mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E comparing the phenotypes of two different sgRNAs.

claim: At 20 dph, female ndrg1b mutants showed a decrease in the number of oogonia and pre-vitellogenic oocytes compared to wt individuals.
source: Histological examination showed ovaries with apparently normal development (Figure 3B); however, there is a decrease in the number of oogonia and pre-vitellogenic oocytes compared to wt individuals (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and cell quantification data shown in Figures 3B, D, and E.

claim: At 20 dph, male ndrg1b mutants showed a significant reduction of cysts and germ cells within the cyst in relation to wt males.
source: In males, the mutant showed a significant reduction of cysts and germ cells within the cyst in relation to wt males (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and cell quantification data shown in Figures 3F and G.

claim: Germ cell number is affected in ndrg1b mutants for both sexes at times that are key to the commitment of type II cyst division.
source: This indicates that germ cell number is affected in ndrg1b mutants for both sexes at times that are key to the commitment of type II cyst division.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing reduced germ cell numbers in both sexes at 20 dph, which is a critical time for type II cyst division.

claim: The ndrg1b mutant females spawned fewer eggs than wt females.
source: Regarding the daily frequency of spawning, the ndrg1b mutant females spawned fewer eggs than wt females (Figure 4B), although fertilization rate was normal (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reproductive success data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The fertilization rate was normal in ndrg1b mutant females paired with wt males.
source: Regarding the daily frequency of spawning, the ndrg1b mutant females spawned fewer eggs than wt females (Figure 4B), although fertilization rate was normal (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reproductive success data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The wt females paired with male sgN1b spawned fewer oocytes.
source: Surprisingly, the wt females paired with male sgN1b also spawned fewer oocytes (Figure 4B), and in sgN1b males paired with wt females, the fertilization rate declined (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reproductive success data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In sgN1b males paired with wt females, the fertilization rate declined.
source: Surprisingly, the wt females paired with male sgN1b also spawned fewer oocytes (Figure 4B), and in sgN1b males paired with wt females, the fertilization rate declined (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reproductive success data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hatching rate was lower for the progeny of male sgN1b and wt female than for the progeny of female sgN1b and wt male.
source: Moreover, hatching rate was lower for the progeny of male sgN1b and wt female than for the progeny of female sgN1b and wt male (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reproductive success data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All ndrg1b mutants invariably displayed typical female and male secondary sex characteristics.
source: Medaka adults display easily distinguishable secondary sex characteristics, for example, the hindmost rays are separated from other rays in the dorsal fin in the male, but linked together in female. All ndrg1b mutants invariably displayed typical female and male secondary sex characteristics (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations shown in Figures 4E–H.

claim: A balanced sex ratio was observed in both ndrg1b mutants and wt individuals.
source: A balanced sex ratio was observed in both ndrg1b mutants and wt individuals (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sex ratio data presented in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Female ndrg1b mutants had significantly fewer oogonia, pre-vitellogenic, and vitellogenic oocytes at the different stages than wt individuals.
source: Histological examination of females showed ovaries with apparently normal development (Figure 4I), but there were significantly fewer oogonia, pre-vitellogenic, and vitellogenic oocytes at the different stages in ndrg1b mutants than in wt individuals (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis and cell quantification data shown in Figures 4I, K, L, and M.

claim: All stages of spermatogenesis were observed in sgN1b mutants.
source: With respect to the histological examination of testis, all stages of spermatogenesis were observed in sgN1b mutants (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The number of cysts containing spermatogonia remained unchanged in sgN1b males compared to wt.
source: When these cells were counted manually, the number of cysts containing spermatogonia remained unchanged (Figure 4N); however, the number of spermatogonia within each cyst was lower in sgN1b than in wt individuals (Figure 4O), and the total number of spermatozoa was lower in sgN1b testes than in wt testes (Figure 4P).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The number of spermatogonia within each cyst was lower in sgN1b than in wt individuals.
source: When these cells were counted manually, the number of cysts containing spermatogonia remained unchanged (Figure 4N); however, the number of spermatogonia within each cyst was lower in sgN1b than in wt individuals (Figure 4O), and the total number of spermatozoa was lower in sgN1b testes than in wt testes (Figure 4P).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: The total number of spermatozoa was lower in sgN1b testes than in wt testes.
source: When these cells were counted manually, the number of cysts containing spermatogonia remained unchanged (Figure 4N); however, the number of spermatogonia within each cyst was lower in sgN1b than in wt individuals (Figure 4O), and the total number of spermatozoa was lower in sgN1b testes than in wt testes (Figure 4P).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell quantification data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: Alterations of cystic proliferation, with the concomitant lower sperm count and fewer oocytes, have direct influence on reproduction.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that alterations of cystic proliferation, with the concomitant lower sperm count and fewer oocytes, have direct influence on reproduction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing reduced gamete production and reduced reproductive success in mutants.

claim: Alterations of cystic proliferation in ndrg1b mutants do not change the general gonadal morphology or secondary sex characteristics in either sex or the sex ratio.
source: Interestingly, these alterations do not change the general gonadal morphology or secondary sex characteristics in either sex or the sex ratio.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing normal gonadal structure, normal secondary sex characteristics, and balanced sex ratio despite reduced gamete production.

claim: All couples displayed the usual actions of sexual behavior, with differences observed only in the actions related to mating behavior.
source: In general, all couples displayed the usual actions of sexual behavior (Figure 5B–I), with differences observed only in the actions related to mating behavior, particularly in the wrapping actions related to the stimulation of the female spawning, the duration of quivering, and number of convulsions, which were significantly fewer in sgN1b males paired with wt females than in control couples (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figures 5B–I.

claim: The duration of quivering was significantly lower in sgN1b males paired with wt females than in control couples.
source: In general, all couples displayed the usual actions of sexual behavior (Figure 5B–I), with differences observed only in the actions related to mating behavior, particularly in the wrapping actions related to the stimulation of the female spawning, the duration of quivering, and number of convulsions, which were significantly fewer in sgN1b males paired with wt females than in control couples (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The number of convulsions was significantly fewer in sgN1b males paired with wt females than in control couples.
source: In general, all couples displayed the usual actions of sexual behavior (Figure 5B–I), with differences observed only in the actions related to mating behavior, particularly in the wrapping actions related to the stimulation of the female spawning, the duration of quivering, and number of convulsions, which were significantly fewer in sgN1b males paired with wt females than in control couples (Figure 5H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Alterations of cystic proliferation, with the concomitant lower sperm count, have direct influence on reproduction and mating behavior.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that alterations of cystic proliferation, with the concomitant lower sperm count, have direct influence on reproduction and mating behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing reduced sperm count, reduced reproductive success, and altered mating behavior in mutants.

claim: The 11-ketotestosterone (11-KT) quantification did not show differences between wt and sgN1b males in a reproductive trial.
source: The 11-ketotestosterone (11-KT) quantification did not show differences between wt and sgN1b males in a reproductive trial (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B), supporting that reduction in cystic proliferation and a reduced number of germ cells in males would not affect sex steroid-producing somatic cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by 11-KT quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Reduction in cystic proliferation and a reduced number of germ cells in males would not affect sex steroid-producing somatic cells.
source: The 11-ketotestosterone (11-KT) quantification did not show differences between wt and sgN1b males in a reproductive trial (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B), supporting that reduction in cystic proliferation and a reduced number of germ cells in males would not affect sex steroid-producing somatic cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the 11-KT data showing no difference between wt and mutant males.

claim: The expression of ndrg1b is restricted to the gonad, not being observed in the brain.
source: We observed that the expression of ndrg1b is restricted to the gonad (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B), not being observed in the brain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B, and E.

claim: Within the testis, ndrg1b was observed in presumptive A-type undifferentiated spermatogonia (SGa).
source: Within the testis, ndrg1b was observed in presumptive A-type undifferentiated spermatogonia (SGa; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) since the cells that presented ndrg1b marking are situated in the most peripheral region of the tubule, where oct4-positive cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C) or SGa are observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C, and D.

claim: Ndrg1 homologs have been found in different species of invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Ndrg1 homologs have been found in different species of invertebrates and vertebrates (Fang et al., 2014; Kovacevic et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Fang et al., 2014; Kovacevic et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013).

claim: In mammals, Ndrg1 exerts an inhibitory effect on cancer cell proliferation.
source: In mammals, it has been well established that Ndrg1 exerts an inhibitory effect on cancer cell proliferation (Chang et al., 2014; McCaig et al., 2011; Xi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chang et al., 2014; McCaig et al., 2011; Xi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).

claim: Ndrg1 is expressed in the gonads of humans, mice, sheep, and medaka.
source: Additionally, several studies have shown that Ndrg1 is expressed in the gonads of humans, mice, sheep, and medaka (Burl et al., 2018; Kikuchi et al., 2019; Lachat et al., 2002; Qu et al., 2019; Stévant and Nef, 2019); however, its role in gonadal function and reproduction is still unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Burl et al., 2018; Kikuchi et al., 2019; Lachat et al., 2002; Qu et al., 2019; Stévant and Nef, 2019).

claim: The role of Ndrg1 in gonadal function and reproduction is still unknown.
source: Additionally, several studies have shown that Ndrg1 is expressed in the gonads of humans, mice, sheep, and medaka (Burl et al., 2018; Kikuchi et al., 2019; Lachat et al., 2002; Qu et al., 2019; Stévant and Nef, 2019); however, its role in gonadal function and reproduction is still unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: Cystic division is a highly conserved mechanism that precedes gametogenesis in both invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Cystic division is a highly conserved mechanism that precedes gametogenesis in both invertebrates and vertebrates (Amini et al., 2014; Hansen and Schedl, 2006; Hinnant et al., 2017; Lei and Spradling, 2013a; Quagio-Grassiotto et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Amini et al., 2014; Hansen and Schedl, 2006; Hinnant et al., 2017; Lei and Spradling, 2013a; Quagio-Grassiotto et al., 2011).

claim: Obtaining a mutant line for ndrg1b was not possible because in homozygosis it would appear to be lethal.
source: However, obtaining a mutant line for ndrg1b was not possible because in homozygosis it would appear to be lethal.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of homozygous mutants in the F2 generation.

claim: Individuals died during embryonic early development for unknown reason when homozygous for ndrg1b mutation.
source: From the analysis of F2 individuals, and waiting for the presence of 25% homozygous KOs to ndrg1b, surprisingly, this genotype was not obtained because individuals died during embryonic early development for unknown reason.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of homozygous mutants in the F2 generation.

claim: In fish, and especially in medaka, the complex Cas9/sgRNA generated a high-efficiency biallelic mutations of injected animals.
source: In fish, and especially in medaka (Ansai and Kinoshita, 2014), it has been well established that the complex Cas9/sgRNA generated a high-efficiency biallelic mutations of injected animals (cas9+sgRNA).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ansai and Kinoshita, 2014.

claim: The high efficiency of biallelic mutant and the use of this approach to research in medaka were already corroborated recently in our laboratory.
source: The high efficiency of biallelic mutant and the use of this approach to research in medaka were already corroborated recently in our laboratory (Castañeda Cortés et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Castañeda Cortés et al., 2019).

claim: In a previous study using biallelic mutants of crhr1 and crhr2, no relevant gonadal phenotype was observed in biallelic mutant fish reared at 24°C.
source: Furthermore, in a previous study by Castañeda Cortés et al., 2019 in medaka using biallelic mutants of two different sgRNAs targeting other loci, the corticotropin-releasing hormone receptors (crhr1 and crhr2), no relevant gonadal phenotype was observed in biallelic mutant fish reared at 24°C, showing the lack of a relevant phenotype in the germline after the use of CRISPR/Cas9.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Castañeda Cortés et al., 2019.

claim: ndrg1b is likely involved in the molecular regulation of cystic division in medaka.
source: In the present study, we generated ndrg1b F0 mutants by using CRISPR/Cas9 technology and showed that the lack of ndrg1b leads to a reduction in the total number of germ cells by inhibiting cystic proliferation in both sexes during early gonadal development and adulthood. This is evidence that ndrg1b is likely involved in the molecular regulation of cystic division in medaka.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that loss of ndrg1b function leads to reduced cystic proliferation.

claim: Type II proliferation (cystic) is crucial to gamete production, and consequently, to related reproductive parameters such as the number of spawned eggs, spermatozoa, and fertilization rate.
source: In this regard, although a previous study has shown that type I proliferation is important to germline stem cell number in adult medaka gonads (Morinaga et al., 2007), here we showed that type II proliferation (cystic) is also crucial to gamete production, and consequently, to related reproductive parameters such as the number of spawned eggs, spermatozoa, and fertilization rate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing reduced gamete production and reproductive success in ndrg1b mutants with impaired type II proliferation.

claim: Expression of ndrg1b in testis is restricted to the most peripheral region of the tubule, where A-type undifferentiated spermatogonia (SGa) are present.
source: Moreover, expression of ndrg1b in testis is restricted to the most peripheral region of the tubule, where A-type undifferentiated spermatogonia (SGa) are present (Iwai et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and citation to Iwai et al., 2006 for the location of SGa.

claim: The reduction of cystic proliferation in ndrg1b mutants did not induce any sex reversal or modification in the sex ratio.
source: Additionally, we observed that the reduction of cystic proliferation in ndrg1b mutants did not induce any sex reversal or modification in the sex ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing normal secondary sex characteristics and balanced sex ratio in mutants.

claim: The mechanism underlying sex reversal is manifested before germline cells exit from the status of stem cells/gonocytes and enter the gametogenic program.
source: These observations are in agreement with Nishimura et al., 2018 in figla, meioC, and dazl mutants in medaka, in which follicle formation is disrupted, germ cells are unable to commit to gametogenesis, and germ cells do not develop into EGSCs, respectively. All these mutants exhibited female secondary characteristics and ovary structures, demonstrating that the mechanism underlying sex reversal is manifested before germline cells exit from the status of stem cells/gonocytes and enter the gametogenic program (Nishimura et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nishimura et al., 2018.

claim: Medaka mutants that had an effect on type I proliferation showed sex reversal.
source: In contrast, medaka mutants that had an effect on type I proliferation, like the germ cell-deficient cxcr4 (Kurokawa et al., 2007) and also loss of amhrII (TGF-β pathway member) that display hyperproliferative germ cells (Morinaga et al., 2007; Nakamura et al., 2012), showed sex reversal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kurokawa et al., 2007; Morinaga et al., 2007; Nakamura et al., 2012).

claim: The TGF-β pathway is not involved in the cystic division.
source: Interestingly, our results showed that the TGF-β pathway is not involved in the cystic division, and the increased proliferation in males is due to inhibition of TGF-β members involved in controlling germ cell type I proliferation, such as amh.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that TGF-β inhibition affects type I but not type II proliferation.

claim: The increased proliferation in males following TGF-β inhibition is due to inhibition of TGF-β members involved in controlling germ cell type I proliferation, such as amh.
source: Interestingly, our results showed that the TGF-β pathway is not involved in the cystic division, and the increased proliferation in males is due to inhibition of TGF-β members involved in controlling germ cell type I proliferation, such as amh.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and knowledge of TGF-β pathway members.

claim: Sexual behavior is linked to reproductive success.
source: It has been established that sexual behavior is linked to reproductive success (Oshima et al., 2003), and, fortunately, the sexual behavior of medaka consists of a sequence of several actions that are easily quantified (Ono and Uematsu, 1957; Walter and Hamilton, 1970).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Oshima et al., 2003; Ono and Uematsu, 1957; Walter and Hamilton, 1970).

claim: Ejaculation in male rats is accompanied by strong vibration and significant abdominal contraction.
source: We specifically observed differences in male mating behavior related to stimulation of female spawning and fertilization, such as the duration of quivering and number of convulsions; actions that seem to be conserved in vertebrates because ejaculation in male rats is accompanied by strong vibration and significant abdominal contraction (Qin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Qin et al., 2017.

claim: Sexual behavior has been found to be strongly controlled by the brain and levels of sex steroid hormones.
source: Sexual behavior has been found to be strongly controlled by the brain (Hiraki-Kajiyama et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2020; Yang and Shah, 2014) and levels of sex steroid hormones (Hiraki-Kajiyama et al., 2019; Munakata and Kobayashi, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hiraki-Kajiyama et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2020; Yang and Shah, 2014; Munakata and Kobayashi, 2010).

claim: In medaka, the secondary sex characters are induced by sex steroid hormones.
source: Here, it is important to note that in medaka the secondary sex characters are induced by sex steroid hormones (Kikuchi et al., 2019; Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kikuchi et al., 2019; Sato et al., 2008).

claim: Sex steroid synthesis is not impaired in ndrg1b mutants.
source: ndrg1b mutants showed normal secondary sex characters in both males and females. Moreover, the level of the main androgen in fish, 11-KT, did not show differences between wt and ndrg1b mutants, thus establishing that sex steroid synthesis is not impaired in these animals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing normal secondary sex characteristics and normal 11-KT levels in mutants.

claim: In studies where the regulation of sex hormones was altered, changes in sexual behavior were primarily related to courtship.
source: Regarding sexual behavior, in studies where the regulation of sex hormones was altered, changes in sexual behavior were primarily related to courtship, such as the frequencies of following, dancing, and latency from the first courtship (Hiraki-Kajiyama et al., 2019; Oshima et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hiraki-Kajiyama et al., 2019; Oshima et al., 2003).

claim: When brain regulators were altered, changes in courtship display and sexual motivation, latency to mating and number of courtships displays, and latency to mating were observed.
source: Additionally, when brain regulators were altered, such as arginine-vasotocin (Yokoi et al., 2015), oxytocin ligand (oxt) (Yokoi et al., 2020), and TN-GnRH3 (Okuyama et al., 2014), changes in courtship display and sexual motivation, latency to mating and number of courtships displays, and latency to mating were observed, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Yokoi et al., 2015; Yokoi et al., 2020; Okuyama et al., 2014).

claim: None of the courtship actions changed in the male ndrg1b mutants.
source: None of these courtship actions changed in the male ndrg1b mutants, leading us to consider whether the specific mating actions of quivering and convulsions are exclusively related to the lower number of spermatogonia and spermatozoa in males.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral analysis data showing no changes in courtship behaviors.

claim: Successive multiple mating-induced depletion of sperm reserves decreased fertilization and mating rate, and females responded by reducing clutch size.
source: To our knowledge, only one other study has observed this loss of mating vigor in medaka. In it, successive multiple mating-induced depletion of sperm reserves decreased fertilization and mating rate, and even females responded by reducing clutch size (Weir and Grant, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weir and Grant, 2010.

claim: Mutations of ndrg1b lead to disruption of germline stem cell cystic proliferation with a subsequent reduction in the number of gametes and an unexpected change in mating behavior of medaka.
source: Taken together, our data show that mutations of ndrg1b lead to disruption of germline stem cell cystic proliferation with a subsequent reduction in the number of gametes and an unexpected change in mating behavior of medaka.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: ndrg1b is involved in the regulation of cystic proliferation during different stages of medaka development (embryo, juvenile, and adult) in a TGF-β-independent manner.
source: Altogether, these data are significant for three main reasons: (1) we showed that ndrg1b is involved in the regulation of cystic proliferation during different stages of medaka development (embryo, juvenile, and adult) in a TGF-β-independent manner
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data across different developmental stages and the TGF-β inhibition experiments.

claim: Mutation of ndrg1b leads to changes in number of gametes, decreasing reproductive success for both sexes.
source: (2) we demonstrated that mutation of ndrg1b leads to changes in number of gametes, decreasing reproductive success for both sexes
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding of the study, supported by the gamete quantification and reproductive success data.

claim: ndrg1b mutation affected male mating behaviors in medaka without changing androgen production.
source: (3) ndrg1b mutation affected male mating behaviors in medaka without changing androgen production.
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding of the study, supported by the behavioral analysis and 11-KT quantification data.

claim: Proliferation of embryonic germline stem cells (EGSCs) gives rise to a cohort of germ cells that will ultimately form the primary population of germ cells in the gonads of both sexes.
source: Proliferation of embryonic germline stem cells (EGSCs, the name applied to PGCs after they reach the gonadal primordium) gives rise to a cohort of germ cells that will ultimately form the primary population of germ cells in the gonads of both sexes (Tanaka, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tanaka, 2019.

claim: Type I proliferation is similar to the self-renewal of germline stem cells in the adult ovary or testis.
source: This type of slow, intermittent division, also called type I proliferation, is similar to the self-renewal of germline stem cells in the adult ovary or testis (Chen and Liu, 2015; Nakamura et al., 2010), and is responsible for ensuring the production of the correct number of germline stem cells that will initiate gametogenesis (Tanaka, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Liu, 2015; Nakamura et al., 2010; and Tanaka, 2019.

claim: Type I proliferation is responsible for ensuring the production of the correct number of germline stem cells that will initiate gametogenesis.
source: This type of slow, intermittent division, also called type I proliferation, is similar to the self-renewal of germline stem cells in the adult ovary or testis (Chen and Liu, 2015; Nakamura et al., 2010), and is responsible for ensuring the production of the correct number of germline stem cells that will initiate gametogenesis (Tanaka, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tanaka, 2019.

claim: The hyperproliferation of mitotically active germ cells in hotei medaka induces 50% male-to-female sex reversal and loss of reproductive success in adult fish.
source: In addition, the hyperproliferation of mitotically active germ cells in hotei medaka, a mutant fish for anti-Müllerian hormone receptor II (amhrII), induces 50% male-to-female sex reversal and loss of reproductive success in adult fish (Morinaga et al., 2007; Nakamura et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Morinaga et al., 2007 and Nakamura et al., 2012.

claim: Lack of EGSC proliferation during the embryo stage induces male-to-female sex reversal in zebrafish and medaka.
source: On the contrary, lack of this proliferation of EGSCs during the embryo stage induces the opposite sex reversal in zebrafish and medaka (Kurokawa et al., 2007; Rodríguez-Marí et al., 2010), showing that this initial proliferation can be also involved in gonadal sex fate.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kurokawa et al., 2007 and Rodríguez-Marí et al., 2010.

claim: Initial EGSC proliferation can be involved in gonadal sex fate.
source: On the contrary, lack of this proliferation of EGSCs during the embryo stage induces the opposite sex reversal in zebrafish and medaka (Kurokawa et al., 2007; Rodríguez-Marí et al., 2010), showing that this initial proliferation can be also involved in gonadal sex fate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited studies showing that lack of EGSC proliferation causes sex reversal.

claim: A second EGSC proliferation occurs prior to meiosis, following a special program of synchronous, successive and incomplete mitosis, generating interconnected daughter cells known as cysts or nests.
source: A second EGSC proliferation occurs prior to meiosis, following a special program of synchronous, successive and incomplete mitosis, generating interconnected daughter cells known as cysts or nests, which are surrounded by somatic cells (Saito et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Saito et al., 2007.

claim: Following several rounds of mitosis, the cells enter meiosis to become oocytes in the ovary or spermatocytes in the testis.
source: Following several rounds of mitosis, the cells enter meiosis to become oocytes in the ovary or spermatocytes in the testis (Lei and Spradling, 2013b; Matova and Cooley, 2001; Tanaka, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lei and Spradling, 2013b; Matova and Cooley, 2001; and Tanaka, 2016.

claim: Female germ cells enter meiosis earlier, while male germ cells are arrested and undergo meiosis at the onset of the prepubertal period.
source: It has been well established in vertebrates that female germ cells enter meiosis earlier, while male germ cells are arrested and undergo meiosis at the onset of the prepubertal period (Elkouby and Mullins, 2017; Koubova et al., 2006; Lei and Spradling, 2013a; Pepling, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elkouby and Mullins, 2017; Koubova et al., 2006; Lei and Spradling, 2013a; and Pepling, 2006.

claim: In medaka, type II proliferation in females increases the number of EGSCs dramatically during embryonic stages, whereas in males, this exponential proliferation to form cysts begins later, in the juvenile stage.
source: In medaka, this type of cystic cell division is known as type II proliferation, by which, in females, the number of EGSCs increases dramatically during embryonic stages; whereas in males, this exponential proliferation to form cysts begins later, in the juvenile stage (Satoh and Egami, 1972; Tanaka, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Satoh and Egami, 1972 and Tanaka, 2019.

claim: Cystic cell proliferation during early life is not fully understood at the molecular level.
source: Despite the importance of cystic cell proliferation during early life to ensure reproductive success, this process is not fully understood at the molecular level (Elkouby and Mullins, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Elkouby and Mullins, 2017.

claim: ndrg1 was found to be upregulated in germ cells with mutated foxl3.
source: In the search for genes that regulate EGSCs proliferation, ndrg1 (n-myc downstream regulated gene 1) is one of the genes that was found to be upregulated in germ cells with mutated foxl3, a switch gene involved in the germline sexual fate decision in medaka (Kikuchi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kikuchi et al., 2019.

claim: Ndrg1 is involved in the regulation of cell proliferation in different cancers.
source: Interestingly, Ndrg1 is involved in the regulation of cell proliferation in different cancers (Chang et al., 2014; McCaig et al., 2011; Xi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2014; McCaig et al., 2011; Xi et al., 2017; and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: NDRG1 is highly conserved among species from mammals to fish, C. elegans to fruit fly.
source: Moreover, this gene has homologs from mammals (Ndrg1) to fish (ndrg1), Caenorhabditis elegans (ZK1073.1) to fruit fly (Dmel\MESK2), suggesting that NDRG1 is highly conserved among species (Kovacevic et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kovacevic et al., 2013 and Sun et al., 2013.

claim: Ndrg1 has been demonstrated to inhibit the TGF-β signaling cascade.
source: Ndrg1 has been demonstrated to inhibit the TGF-β signaling cascade, a very well-known pathway involved in cell proliferation and survival (Zhang et al., 2017), regulating the induction of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in mammalian cells (Tojo et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2014), establishing ndrg1 as a potent inhibitor of proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2017; Tojo et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2012; and Jin et al., 2014.

claim: ndrg1 is established as a potent inhibitor of proliferation.
source: Ndrg1 has been demonstrated to inhibit the TGF-β signaling cascade, a very well-known pathway involved in cell proliferation and survival (Zhang et al., 2017), regulating the induction of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in mammalian cells (Tojo et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2014), establishing ndrg1 as a potent inhibitor of proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited studies showing ndrg1's inhibitory effects on proliferation-related pathways.

claim: The role of ndrg1 in non-cancerous cells is not well established.
source: However, its role in non-cancerous cells is not well established.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: The production of an adequate number of gametes is necessary for normal reproduction.
source: The production of an adequate number of gametes is necessary for normal reproduction, for which the regulation of proliferation from early gonadal development to adulthood is key in both sexes.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: The regulation of proliferation from early gonadal development to adulthood is key in both sexes for normal reproduction.
source: The production of an adequate number of gametes is necessary for normal reproduction, for which the regulation of proliferation from early gonadal development to adulthood is key in both sexes.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Cystic proliferation of germline stem cells is an especially important step prior to the beginning of meiosis.
source: Cystic proliferation of germline stem cells is an especially important step prior to the beginning of meiosis; however, the molecular regulators of this proliferation remain elusive in vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge and the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The molecular regulators of cystic proliferation remain elusive in vertebrates.
source: Cystic proliferation of germline stem cells is an especially important step prior to the beginning of meiosis; however, the molecular regulators of this proliferation remain elusive in vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: ndrg1b is an important regulator of cystic proliferation in medaka.
source: Here, we report that ndrg1b is an important regulator of cystic proliferation in medaka.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Mutants of ndrg1b led to a disruption of cystic proliferation of germ cells.
source: We generated mutants of ndrg1b that led to a disruption of cystic proliferation of germ cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing reduced cystic proliferation in mutants.

claim: The loss of cystic proliferation was observed from embryogenic to adult stages in ndrg1b mutants.
source: This loss of cystic proliferation was observed from embryogenic to adult stages, impacting the success of gamete production and reproductive parameters such as spawning and fertilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data across different developmental stages.

claim: The loss of cystic proliferation in ndrg1b mutants impacted the success of gamete production and reproductive parameters such as spawning and fertilization.
source: This loss of cystic proliferation was observed from embryogenic to adult stages, impacting the success of gamete production and reproductive parameters such as spawning and fertilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing reduced gamete production and reproductive success.

claim: The depletion of cystic proliferation impacted male sexual behavior, with a decrease of mating vigor.
source: Interestingly, the depletion of cystic proliferation also impacted male sexual behavior, with a decrease of mating vigor.
evidence: The claim is supported by the behavioral analysis data showing reduced mating behaviors in mutant males.

claim: It is necessary to consider gamete production capacity in order to analyze reproductive behavior.
source: These data illustrate why it is also necessary to consider gamete production capacity in order to analyze reproductive behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's findings showing a link between gamete production and mating behavior.

claim: Cell division and differentiation are well-controlled processes for the development of a functional organ in multicellular organisms.
source: Cell division and differentiation are well-controlled processes for the development of a functional organ in multicellular organisms.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.

claim: In gonads, cell division and differentiation processes are essential to guarantee the correct production of gametes necessary for successful reproduction.
source: In gonads, these processes are also essential to guarantee the correct production of gametes necessary for successful reproduction (Lombardi, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lombardi, 1998.

claim: Vertebrate gonads acquire sex-specific features during gonadogenesis.
source: Vertebrate gonads acquire sex-specific features during gonadogenesis, an exceptional, complex, multistep process that includes migration of primordial germ cells (PGCs) to reach the gonadal primordium, proliferation, differentiation, and meiosis (DeFalco and Capel, 2009; Richardson and Lehmann, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DeFalco and Capel, 2009 and Richardson and Lehmann, 2010.

claim: Gonadogenesis is an exceptional, complex, multistep process that includes migration of primordial germ cells to reach the gonadal primordium, proliferation, differentiation, and meiosis.
source: Vertebrate gonads acquire sex-specific features during gonadogenesis, an exceptional, complex, multistep process that includes migration of primordial germ cells (PGCs) to reach the gonadal primordium, proliferation, differentiation, and meiosis (DeFalco and Capel, 2009; Richardson and Lehmann, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DeFalco and Capel, 2009 and Richardson and Lehmann, 2010.

claim: Defects in any of the gonadogenesis steps may lead to sex abnormalities including infertility and sex reversal.
source: Defects in any of these steps may lead to sex abnormalities including infertility and sex reversal.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge.
